title: Systems and architecture
note: Design starts with orders of magnitude: a memory reference is about 100 ns, a datacenter round trip about 0.5 ms, a disk seek about 10 ms, and a cross-ocean round trip about 150 ms. Systems scale by adding machines behind load balancers, caching hot data, queuing slow work, and measuring everything.

read.title: Think in orders of magnitude
text: A widely shared table of latencies, credited to Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig, is worth memorizing roughly. Reading from L1 cache takes about a nanosecond and from main memory about 100. A round trip inside a datacenter costs about half a millisecond, a spinning-disk seek about 10 milliseconds, and a packet from California to the Netherlands and back about 150 milliseconds. The lesson is that a single network hop costs thousands of memory reads, so architecture is often about avoiding trips.

Caching attacks that cost directly by keeping hot data close. The common cache-aside pattern checks the cache first and, on a miss, reads the database and stores the result with a time to live. Queues attack it differently: work that does not need an immediate answer, such as sending email, goes onto a queue, and workers process it at their own pace. Because most queues deliver at least once, consumers must handle duplicates safely.

Splitting a monolith into microservices lets teams deploy and scale parts independently, but every call that was a function call becomes a network call that can be slow or fail. That is why distributed systems lean on observability: metrics for trends, logs for detail, and traces to follow one request across services.

q.q: What lesson does the reading draw from the latency table?
o: A network hop costs thousands of memory reads

q.q: Why must queue consumers handle duplicates?
o: Most queues deliver messages at least once

q.q: What new cost appears when a monolith becomes microservices?
o: Teams can no longer deploy separately
Function calls become network calls that can fail
